items.context: A rough lump on the finger for months.

img.author: CDC/ Richard S. Hibbets (cropped)
img.alt: A finger with a round, rough, raised growth on its back.

items.why: A rough, raised papule with a cauliflower surface: verruca vulgaris from HPV.
items.pearl: Most warts go away on their own within two years. Freezing or salicylic acid can speed things up.

items.context: Gums bleed when brushing. No pain.

img.author: CDC (cropped)
img.alt: Front teeth with red, puffy gum margins.

items.why: Red, swollen gum margins that bleed easily, with no loss of the bone holding the teeth.
items.pearl: Fully reversible with good brushing and flossing. Left alone, it can progress to periodontitis and loose teeth.

items.context: Stung while gardening near a mound of small reddish ants.

img.author: CDC/ Harold George Scott, PhD (cropped)
img.alt: Hairy skin with a small red bump topped by a white pustule.

items.why: A sterile white pustule on a red base that forms within a day of a fire ant sting.
items.pearl: Red imported fire ants are spreading in south-east Queensland and have been found in NSW; report suspected nests.

items.context: A child with fever, sore throat and a sandpaper rash.

img.author: CDC/ Heinz F. Eichenwald, MD (cropped)
img.alt: Open mouth with a red throat and a tongue with a white coat dotted by red papillae.

items.why: Swollen red papillae poking through a white coat on the tongue.
items.pearl: Classic in scarlet fever, but also in Kawasaki disease and toxic shock syndrome. The white coat peels to a red tongue after a few days.

items.context: Weeks of broad-spectrum antibiotics and barely eating. Now large bruises.

img.author: CDC (cropped)
img.alt: An upper arm with several large purple bruises.

items.why: Large bruises from too little vitamin K to make clotting factors.
items.pearl: Factors II, VII, IX and X need vitamin K, so the INR rises. It's why newborns get vitamin K at birth.

items.context: Blisters on the neck the morning after swatting a beetle on a summer night.

img.author: CDC/ Dr. Henry D. Pratt
img.alt: Skin of the neck with several clear, fluid-filled blisters.

items.why: Clear blisters where a crushed beetle released the blistering chemical cantharidin.
items.pearl: Cantharidin from these beetles is also used on purpose, in tiny doses, to treat warts and molluscum.

items.context: A farm worker with a tender, boggy lump on the back of the neck.

img.author: CDC/ Dr. Lucille K. Georg
img.alt: Back of a neck with a raised, round, swollen plaque with hair loss.

items.why: A boggy, inflamed plaque with hair loss from a fungus caught from cattle.
items.pearl: Often mistaken for an abscess. It needs oral antifungals, not cutting; draining it doesn't help.

items.context: A barefoot farmer from volcanic highlands with years of swollen, warty feet.

img.author: CDC/ Dr. Martin D. Hicklin
img.alt: A swollen foot with thickened, warty, moss-like skin over the toes.

items.why: Warty, 'mossy' swelling of both feet from years of barefoot contact with volcanic clay soil.
items.pearl: A non-infectious elephantiasis, entirely preventable with shoes and foot hygiene.

items.context: Fever and headache a week after camping near Litchfield, NT.

img.author: CDC/ Margaret A. Parsons
img.alt: Skin with a small black-crusted sore on a red base.

items.why: A painless black scab where an infected mite larva fed: the calling card of Orientia tsutsugamushi.
items.pearl: Found in far north Queensland, the Torres Strait and the Top End. Doxycycline works fast, so look hard for an eschar in skin folds.

items.context: Rough, bumpy skin on the elbows of a man living on a very limited diet.

img.author: CDC
img.alt: Skin of the elbow covered in many tiny raised, spiky bumps.

items.why: Dense, horny follicular bumps on the elbows and knees from nutritional deficiency, classically vitamin A.
items.pearl: The name means 'toad skin'. Look for night blindness, dry eyes and a poor diet.
